First Chapter.
Dwelling on the peak of Mount Kailāsa, the Destroyer of Time (Kāla), the Treasure-Trove of Compassion.
Mahādeva, the Great Lord, is the support of boundless majesty. || 1 ||
The support of the entire world without exception, the cause of all causes,
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, immeasurable, and undisturbed.
Having approached the Supreme Śiva, who is adorned with his own inconceivable, wondrous, and immeasurable power, the devoted one bowed down and spoke.
Rudra said:
O Ādideva, ocean of compassion, devoted to the fivefold cosmic acts!
Since you are the creator of all, the omniscient, and indeed everything itself.
Therefore, for the benefit of all, you have uttered the Nigamas, Agamas, and Samhitas—primarily consisting of words and their meanings—just like your own breath. (5)
O Blessed One, I have received from your illustrious mouth this which serves as a crown; I now desire to hear its subsequent portion.
(2) "In this [teaching], the supreme dharmas are described as directly bestowing liberation;
for these are the distinguished dharmas of those who observe the Śāmbhava vow.
You have spoken of this previously; now, listen to it from me. (7)
Paraśiva said: Listen, for I shall declare the secret of the *Makuṭottara*,
namely the greatness of the Śāmbhava vow and the daily observance (*āhnika*) for those who observe it.
The specific types of worship, the preparation of the ritual implements for worship,
and the procedure for their final funeral rites are indeed described here in summary.
One who desires to cross the ocean of births, which is agitated by the planets of various miseries, should practice the Śāmbhava vow,
which is known from the conclusions of the Vedas and Āgamas. (10)

(3) They have purified the three impurities—*anādi-mala* and the others—situated within the three bodies; they have dried up the ocean of worldly existence by means of the contemplation of the three *liṅgas*. || 11 ||
All their bonds have been severed by the grace of the auspicious Teacher;
they have attained union with the beloved Lady Liberation, brought to them by the messenger of devotion. || 12 ||

In this [teaching], the piercing (vedha), the mental rite (mānasa-kriyā), and initiation (dīkṣā) are indeed contained within the supreme [state], which shatters the mass of darkness produced by the rising sun of knowledge.
This great secret, the head-vow (śirovratam), is obtained by that very means;
he who, through the union of the equilibrium of karma, shall not be subject to rebirth.
O Rudra, when a person attains immortality through the relationship of means and end between the Śāmbhava vow and liberation,
yet abandons this very vow, he will then reach the end of suffering. 15.
(4) No one lacking merit performs sacrifice for me; no one lacking merit desires liberation;
nor does anyone lacking merit attain the supreme Śāmbhava vow. 16.
One who is devoid of the Śāmbhava vow is merely a bound soul (paśu), even if he is a knower of all scriptures and devoted to the yoga of ritual action;
one who lacks the Śāmbhava vow is declared to be nothing but a bound soul. || 17 ||
He who considers the explanatory praise (arthavāda) regarding the greatness of the Śāmbhava vow to be mere fiction shall indeed experience all forms of torment; of this there is no doubt. (18)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Greatness of the Śāmbhava Vow," in the Kriyāpāda of the illustrious Makutāgama. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
Rudra said:
O Supreme Lord, Soul of All, ocean of perfect qualities!
Recite for me the daily ritual duties to be performed by the followers of the Śāmbhava school.
Paraśiva said:
I shall now proclaim the daily ritual (āhnika) of the Śāmbhavas, which is unsurpassed and which severs the bonds of worldly existence; listen with a focused mind. 2.
Indeed, my devotee, awakening at the hour known as Brahma-muhūrta, should perform his morning duties while recollecting me;
he should touch his eyes with both hands upon his beloved *liṅga*.
Then, having reflected upon the Dharma and its purpose, one should also pay homage to those who possess great lordship.

Whoever beholds at the time of dawn one who observes vows, performs sacrificial sessions, is self-controlled, is devoted, and whose limbs are marked by the sectarian signs, shall obtain his heart's desire. || 4 ||
He who, having risen in the morning, should behold a heretic, a fallen person, a cruel man, one devoid of devotion, or a reviler of the gods, shall encounter misfortune.
(p. 6) Regarding the rules for purification: the wise man should go even far away from his dwelling;
he should wear his sacred thread (*upavīta*) as a penis-string (*liṅgasūtra*), hanging down from behind around his neck.
Having covered his head and wrapped it around, he should perform the voiding of feces and urine.
Then, until mental purity is attained, one should diligently perform purification with clay and water; for one devoid of purification falls downward.
Having washed his feet and hands, he should also perform the ritual rinsing (gaṇḍūṣa).
Reciting the names of the principles (tattvas) known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva,
along with the word Svāhā, the observer of the Śāmbhava vow should sip water in this manner three times.
(p. 7) The procedure for cleaning the teeth, bathing, and so forth:
thereafter, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with twigs such as mango;
having rinsed the mouth and sipped water (ācamana), the wise person should proceed further.
Then, having prepared the Śiva-tīrtha, one should perform the morning bath.
Forming the intention, the recitation of hymns, the sprinkling (mārjana), the Aghamarṣaṇa rite,
and the libation to the deities— this is said to be the fivefold limb of the bath.
One should perform a bath in flowing water, wash the feet of a Brahmin,
recite the Gāyatrī mantra, and offer the arghya oblation while facing the sun;
one should also perform the libation for the gods and sages, and likewise satisfy Yakṣman.
Then, having put on two washed garments that have been exposed to the sun,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the bath with ashes.

Having smeared all the limbs with ashes produced from the fire of Śiva, or else obtained according to the ritual manual, and having performed the ash-bath and the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* mark, one should then veil oneself completely with the ashes.
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) in sequence upon thirty-two locations.
On the head, on the forehead, on the two ears, on the two eyes, on the nose, the mouth, and the throat, and immediately thereafter on the two shoulders. (14)
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart, both sides, the navel, the two private parts, the thighs, the buttocks, and the knees. || 15 ||
There are thirty-two supreme locations on the two calves and the two feet;
thereafter, having consecrated them again, a man should wear the rudrākṣas.
Regarding the wearing of Rudrākṣas:
one should wear a single Rudrākṣa on the crest-lock (śikhā), thirty on the head,
thirty-six on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms.
One may also wear twelve on the wrist and five hundred on the shoulder;
for the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), one should prepare a rosary with one hundred and eight beads.
A man should always wear rudrākṣas while sleeping or eating.
Three hundred is said to be the lowest, five hundred the middle, and one thousand the highest; thus one should maintain [the practice] according to these distinctions. (19)
It should be placed on the head with the Īśāna mantra, on the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
worn on the throat with the Aghora mantra, and likewise on the heart with that same one.
The wise one should hold [the rosary] in his hands with the mantra called Aghora,
and [place it] on his abdomen with the mantra "Vyomavyāpin" together with fifty beads.
One should wear five or seven rosaries with the five Brahma-aṅgas;
or else, one may wear all the beads while reciting the root mantra.
Having offered the arghya to the Sun and performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one should then present three arghyas to the Sun, who is my own form;
thereafter, being self-restrained, one should recite the Sāvitrī, the Goddess who is my deity. (23)
(p. 10) Regarding the worship of the seven tongues of the Śiva-fire:
one should, with self-restraint, worship the fire, which is my terrible form.
[The tongues are] Suvarṇā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā.
The seven tongues are proclaimed to be multiform and exceedingly red. || 24 ||
The tongue in the west is golden; the middle one is known as Kanakā;
the northern tongue is red; and the one situated in the southern direction is black.
Suprabhā is in the eastern direction, Jihvā is extremely red and resides in the domain of Agni, and Bahurūpā is in the northeast; these are the locations of the tongues in successive order.
Vāruṇī is the tongue for marriage, Madhyamā for sacrificial rites,
Uttarā for the initiation ceremony, and Dakṣiṇā for rites for the ancestors.

The eastern direction is recommended for all rites of desire, the southeastern for rites of pacification, and the northeastern for fierce activities; this is always praised for the fire-oblation (homa).
He is endowed with five faces, red in color, and resplendent with seven tongues;
he has ten arms, three eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments. (29)
Clad in red garments and seated upon a lotus, he sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with ten weapons. (30)
Then there is Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and after that Atiraktā; then Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and another, Raktā, who is golden-hued.
The three [lines] are situated facing upwards, while the remaining ones are positioned in the directions starting from the east;
having thus meditated upon Śiva as fire, the wise man should perform the oblation in the evening and the morning.
Having performed the refuge-taking in the Guru and the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), one should then perform the salutation (*abhivādana*).
Listen now to how the taking of refuge in the Guru and others should be performed. (33)
Holding the casket of the *liṅga* firmly with his right hand,
and grasping the Guru’s two big toes with his left hand, he should seek refuge in the Guru and the others three times while touching their eyes. (34)
The duties for the second, third, and fourth parts of the day are as follows:
one should conclude the first eight-part festival in this manner;
and likewise, in the second part, one should practice the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*.
One should recite [the mantra], teach it, and furthermore, investigate the scriptures.
One should gather sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth as they may be obtained;
one should strive for a third portion of one's income for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those who are to be supported. (36)
Then, during the fourth part [of the day], one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing;
having prepared the Śiva-tīrtha, one should then perform the midday bath.
Having performed the midday bath, the twilight worship,
and the ash-bath, one should then apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Likewise, having completed the two midday twilight rites according to the prescribed rule.
Now, the five great sacrifices must be performed daily by the householder.

Having gratified the gods, the sages, and their respective hosts in due order, one should satisfy the divine and non-divine ancestors from the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. Then, having performed the *vaiśvadeva* rite, one should carry out the midday worship. (39)
Regarding the varieties of midday worship:
with a focused mind, I am to be worshipped in a great, medium, or even a brief manner during the six periods of the day, or alternatively, at the three junctions of the day.

When the other [occasion] is indicated as not being a time for eating, one should perform the Great Worship (mahāpūjā) according to the procedure prescribed for the six locations (ṣaṭsthala). || 41 ||

Having placed the chosen liṅga upon the consecrated pedestal of the left hand, which serves as a bed of ashes, and facing north, the practitioner— endowed with meditative visualization and full of concentration— should perform worship with careful attention.
Whether he be a scholar or a fool, a wise man should honor and satisfy a guest who arrives at the conclusion of his own worship, regarding him as me alone. (43)
For even while eating, one should meditate upon me and also recite my name aloud;
there is no impurity in that state, for I am always pure.
Having enjoyed my favor, the devotee of Maheśvara should then,
day after day, wash his face and hands, perform the ācamana twice, and touch his eyes.
Even while reciting hymns in this manner, he should dedicate that food;
and from that, he shall also accomplish his own purpose.
Having performed the evening twilight worship, being self-restrained and pure, he should perform the evening ablution dedicated to Agni;
and having worshipped during the western twilight and completed the fire-oblation, [he should proceed].
One should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite at the evening twilight;
then, having completed the midnight worship, one should honor the guest.
(p. 15) The Procedure for Sleeping at Night:
Then, having reclined upon a comfortable bed, pure and meditating upon me, he should sleep happily, having cast off all worldly thoughts. (49)
I have declared this collection of duties for daily practice which bestows my own state;
those men who do not perform them go to many hells.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Daily Rituals," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Makuta-āgama.
The third chapter.
Rudra said:
O support of immeasurable qualities, O eternal support of the universe!
O Great Guru, now please explain the specific types of worship.
Paraśiva said: Listen, O Rudra, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed varieties of worship.
For worship is declared to be threefold: the heavy (gurvī), the great (mahatī), and the light (laghu). || 2 ||
One should perform the three kinds of worship—
the great, the supreme, the heavy, the middling, and the light— at both evening and midday; however, if one is incapable, one may perform even the light form.
For there are fixed times for non-eating, such as the morning and so forth;
a wise person should perform worship at six periods or, alternatively, at three periods.
Regarding the ritual procedure for the mandala: in the [tantra] called *Avasara*, it is a lotus; in the *Laghu* (Short), it is remembered as nine lotuses;
and in both the *Gurvī* (Long) and the *Mahatī* (Great), it is the *Bhadra*. For the mandala is indeed reality (*tattva*).
p. 17) Regarding the number of wicks (*vartikā*), it is said that for the *avasara* [recitation], three wicks are prescribed;
for the *laghu* [recitation], nine or twelve are further proclaimed.
In the worship of the Guru, thirty-six or eighteen [verses] are prescribed.
One should light either one hundred and eight, three hundred, or even a thousand wicks, even when the transgression is grave or great.
In the *Laghvī* [Kalpa], or during an *avasara*, a single lamp is prescribed;
likewise, four or two lamps are prescribed for the *Mahatī* [Kalpa] and for the Guru as well. (8)
Regarding the rule for the number of recitations:
in the *Laghu-avasara* [rite], one should recite one hundred and eight times;
in both the *Guru* and the *Mahatī* [rites], one should recite the root mantra one thousand times.

O Great-minded One, the three-fold lustration (nīrājana) performed during the festival of Avasarā is said to consist of the lustration known as Darśana, the one known as Uttara, and the one known as Avasarā.
Known as Darśana, known as Avasarākhya, and also known as Majjana;
known as Māṅgalya, Karpūra, Śṛṅgāra, and the great name Mahābhidha. (11)
The rite called Ānanda, which is innumerable, and the nine lustrations (navanīrājana)—these indeed are proclaimed for the abbreviated worship (laghvarcanā). || 12 ||

Along with the previously mentioned [rites], there are eleven offerings of betel-leaves accompanied by affection, as well as solemn lustration ceremonies (nīrājanāni) during the great and weighty [festival].
Without even lighting a lamp, one should not perform any ritual intention;
one should worship the *raṅgavallī* and the lamp with perfumes and other offerings.

O high-minded one, it is proclaimed that the *naivedya* (food offering) is to be presented at the appropriate occasion; however, in the case of the *laghvī* and other [shorter rituals], a *mahānivedana* (great offering) should be performed.
That is declared to be the "great offering" (mahānivedya), which is capable of pacifying hunger;
whereas that offering which is not conducive to the pacification of hunger is merely an occasional offering (avasaranivedya).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Specific Rules for Worship," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Makuta Āgama.
The Fourth Chapter.
Rudra said:
O Śaṅkara, support of inconceivable majesty, ocean of compassion!
Now tell me the method for preparing the substances required for worship.
Paraśiva said:
An ablution with the five nectars and other substances should be performed; [the five are] honey, cow's curd, milk, ghee, and sugar in equal proportions.
For consecration, the most excellent pure water is recommended. || 2 ||
Elā, uśīra, lavaṅga, kastūrī,
and candraka— these five substances— or else *candra*, kastūrī, and *kuṅkuma*, or the pair of elā and uśīra, should be added to the consecration water. || 3 ||
Sandalwood, gorocanā, saffron, cailā, camphor, koṣṭha,
black agallochum, and musk, combined with equal parts of sandalwood. || 4 ||
The powder of either the bilva or the kṛtamāla tree, as well as the fragrance of the devadāru—these are remembered as being dear to me. (5)
Flowers such as the droṇa, the vaka, the punnāga, and likewise the mandāra flower;
the nandyāvarta, the śriyāvarta, the karavīra, and the arka. || 6 ||
The hundred-petaled lotus, the blue water-lily, the lodhra, and the dhattūra;
the pāṭala, the campaka, the bilva, the tamāla, and the karṇikāra. || 7 ||
Mātuluṅga, muni, priyaṅgu, devadāruka, kṛtamāla, agnimantha, mālatī, and likewise mallikā. || 8 ||
Nirguṇḍī, Vikarṇī, Bahuparṇī, and likewise Ajitā;
Kahlāra, Matisīpuṣpa, Kusumbha, and Kamala—these are recommended for my worship; therefore, one should worship me well with them. 9.
Regarding the flowers of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types: indeed, those flowers that are white in color are *sāttvika*.
By offering them to me, they shall grant liberation to my devotees. (10)
Thus, those that are rājasic and reddish in color grant the desired enjoyment;
those that are mixed and yellow in color indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
as well as all desired objects such as sons, grandsons, gold, and so forth.
On this earth, all black things are of the nature of *tamas*, with the exception of the blue lotus;
these must be avoided with effort, for people should not worship me with them. (12)
Flowers that are praised according to the difference of time are the Nandyāvarta, Śriyāvarta, white Arka, white lotus, Lakṣmī, Pāṭala, Punnāga, Mālatī, and likewise the Śaṅkhinī. || 13 ||
The flowers of the palāśa, aśoka, bakula, raktāgastya, and sumana are indeed recommended for worship performed in the morning. (14)
Kṛtamāla, dhattūra, karavīra, droṇaka,
campaka, pāṭala, as well as kamala and utpala—
these are indeed remembered as being praised for worship at the time of midday.
The *jāti*, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), the *kadamba*, the *ketakī*,
the land-lotus (*sthalapadma*), the betel nut (*pūga*), and the flower of the *nāgadantī*—
these indeed are highly recommended for worship performed at midnight. (16)
Gold, the kadamba flower, the ketaki, and the jasmine should be offered at midnight by those devoted to worship; not otherwise.
The *pārijāta* should be used only in the morning, the *candrakāntaka* in the evening, and the *madhyāhnamallikā* should always be employed specifically at midday. (18)
The *trikālamallikā*, as well as golden cloth, the *droṇa* flower, and the *bilva* leaf are indeed always praised. (19)
The flowers to be avoided and those to be accepted are: the yūthikā, the madayantī, the mādhavī, and the śirīṣa;
as well as the bandhūka, the sarjaka, the vibhītaka, and the kunda. (20)
Lāṅgalī, pomegranate, dīpta, nimba, and cotton plant;
kūṣmāṇḍa, śālmalī, matsyākṣī, and the flower of śigru. || 21 ||
Śrīkarṇa, kapittha, and likewise the flower of the tintriṇī—
these should always be avoided by those who desire my grace.
The leaves of bilva, āragvadha, dūrvā, apāmārga, and campaka;
and the leaves of jambu, kadamba, damana, droṇa, and maruvaka. || 23 ||
The leaves of the śaṅkhinī, padma, hrīvera, sindhuvāra, and so forth, are recommended for my worship; with these one should properly worship me. (24)
The bilva leaf is declared to be the most excellent among all leaves;
among flowers, the blue lotus and the karavīra are distinguished as superior;
and the droṇa and āragvadha are indeed the most excellent among all flowers. (25)
Having worshipped with golden leaves and flowers— or with one hundred and eight, or fifty, such golden leaves and flowers— one enjoys infinite fruit. (26)
There is no fault of being "worn-out" (nirmālya) even in the case of golden flowers;
therefore, a devotee should always worship with those [flowers] and leaves.
Golden leaves and flowers, as well as bilva leaves, do not become stale; therefore, one should collect them and perform worship with them.
I shall describe the preparation of various incenses; listen again with focused attention. [Take] camphor, agallochum, takkola, nutmeg, and clove. (29)
Jaṭāmāṃsī, siṃhī, mustā, and sandalwood—this ten-ingredient preparation mixed with ghee is said to be most enchanting. (30)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron,
as well as takkola, cardamom, nāgapuṣpa, and likewise the bark of cloves—
this is indeed known as yakṣakardama, which is pleasing to me. (31)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, clove, cinnamon, and siṃhaka, along with cardamom and jaṭāmāṃsī, is known as the group called Prājāpatya. || 32 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk-mark, as well as clove, nutmeg, and musta—this is proclaimed as that which is called Vijayā. (33)
Camphor, black aloe-wood, hībera, saffron, koṣṭha, and sandalwood, each increasing in quantity in successive order. (34)
This mixture of honey with one, two, three, four, five, or six parts [of other ingredients], known as *śītāri*, is remembered as being pleasing to me. (35)
Having finely powdered sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, siṃhī, sarja resin, koṣṭha, and mustā, and having combined them with that which is called vijayā,
this is celebrated as "Karpūrakalyāṇa," the means for attaining liberation. || 36 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, musk, musta-grass, and lion-urine powder—this is called Amṛta (the Nectar), which bestows the state of immortality. || 37 ||
Takola, pūga, karpūra, jātīphala, and lavaṅgaka—this group known as "fragrant" (sugandha) is considered to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 38 ||
Guggulu alone destroys the sins of seven lifetimes;
likewise, sandalwood incense also annihilates the multitude of all evils.
In this way, fragrant incense accomplishes all desires and goals. (39)
(25) Now, incense made from white aloe-wood alone bestows liberation;
however, incense made from guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter bestows great enjoyment. || 40 ||
Incense made of mahiṣākṣa combined with tamāla powder is pleasing to me; therefore, it bestows union with me. || 41 ||
I shall explain the preparation of the lamp; listen with careful attention.
Cow’s ghee is declared to be the best, while buffalo’s ghee is middling.
O destroyer of Antaka, sesame oil is the lowest for Īśa.
"O son, oil derived from the nimba, eraṇḍa, and karañja trees, as well as that which has a foul odor—none of this should ever be used for my lamp. (43)
One should not perform auspicious rites for the gods or the ancestors without first lighting a lamp; otherwise, they will become fruitless. (44)
Listen attentively, my son, to the characteristics of the five types of threads; I shall now describe the characteristics of the *liṅga*.
One should offer *liṅgas* made of crystal and other materials that are endowed with *śakti*.
One should worship the five-threaded liṅga for the attainment of one's desired goals.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to the length and width of the liṅga and its height;
the gomukha should be half of that; this is proclaimed as the five-sūtra measurement.
If Śiva is in excess, death occurs; if Śakti is in excess, there is loss of wealth.
A Liṅga where Śiva and Śakti are equal bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (47)
One should always carry the desired *liṅga*, which is not less than half a finger-breadth nor more than one finger-breadth in measurement, and which is endowed with five lines.
Regarding the most excellent great liṅga made of clay, which is complete in its parts and bestowed by the Guru,
one should not examine its characteristics, since it has been sanctified by the Guru.
The devotee should mentally visualize the flowers, fruits, and likewise all the ritual materials as being complete, having acquired them according to his own capacity. (50)
That worship which is fulfilled by devotion alone becomes fruitful.
Everything has been stated in brief; what do you wish to hear further?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procurement of Ritual Implements for Worship," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīmakutāgama. || 4 ||
The fifth chapter.
Rudra said:
O Lord, how is there an invocation for you who are omnipresent?
O Lord, how indeed should the installation be performed, and how the placement?
Into which mouth should the food offering (naivedya) be presented? Tell me this.
That which is inedible is called edible by you; it has been reported to you.
Distinguish between for whom it is edible and for whom it would be inedible. (2)
Paraśiva said: Invocation is the invocation consisting of reaching another location, [which is impossible] for me who am all-pervading.
Even if that were not possible, there would still be something further for the agent through his cultivation.
O high-minded one, contemplate that the very manifestation of me in the place conceived as the *liṅga* and so forth is itself the invocation (*āvāhana*).
"Saṃsthāpana" is defined as my own establishment within the heart-lotus of the desired Sadāśiva, whether in the form of a *liṅga*, an image (*bera*), or other such forms. || 5 ||
(29) Proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), cessation (*saṃnirodha*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), and the making of the whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*): proximity is said to be the act of bringing the Self face-to-face.
The prayer for proximity until the end of the worship is "cessation. (6)
That which is the covering with the *kavaca* (armor) is indeed the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*);
the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs] is considered to be the process of making [the deity] complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
The "rendering immortal" (amṛtīkaraṇa) of the five [limbs] beginning with the heart, even though they possess various colors,
consists indeed in the contemplation of them as having my own color.
Regarding the direction the deity faces:
on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and in a mobile liṅga, I face the practitioner;
however, in the case of a water-pot and the like, I face inward, while for a fixed image, I face toward the door.

p. 30) The method of worship for the Five-Faced One should be undertaken by those desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation: "My southern face is [the one] for this; therefore, my worship must indeed be performed facing it. (10)
Together with the arms, heart, secret place, and feet, one should worship me facing upwards by visualizing myself as being turned toward [the practitioner]. || 11 ||
Edibles, foods, drinks, and so forth, as well as various kinds of things to be licked and sucked—
whatever has been prescribed here should be offered with the face turned upwards.
The maintenance of conduct, marks, and so forth, as well as the offering of food (naivedya), is distinguished among the five faces.
Sadyojāta is indeed conduct, while Vāmadeva is remembered as the Guru. (13)
Aghora is declared to be Śiva; Tatpuruṣa would be the mobile [aspect];
Īśāna is grace (prasāda), while I am the distinguished Great One.
Therefore, out of devotion, one should always take all food only after offering it with focused attention to the six emblems, while maintaining a state of serene faith. (15)
Consideration of the Nirmālya:
The nirmālya consumed by me is to be eaten in four ways;
it bestows, in succession, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (16)
The *nirmālya* is stainless, pure, and because of its purity, it is beyond reproach;
therefore, this *nirmālya* must not be consumed by those who are impure and of inauspicious nature. (17)
An impure person, out of greed for purity, attains destruction by consuming what has been eaten by me— which is supremely purifying—
just like the twice-born who consumed the essence.
If one who is addicted to the fickleness of the tongue and devoid of Śaiva consecration eats the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva, he shall go to the Raurava hell. || 19 ||

In this world, those who bear my liṅga, who are my teachers, and who are devoted to me alone—taking me as their sole refuge—it is only in them that [the offering] is appropriate, and not in other living beings. (20)
A fierce [deity] is not authorized;
that which is to be consumed by the fierce is invincible and not intended for enjoyment by others.
[This applies to] the Bāṇaliṅga, the mobile [liṅga], the iron [liṅga], the jewel-liṅga, and the self-manifested (svayambhū) [liṅga].
And in all the images, no fierce person shall be appointed as an attendant. || 21 ||
There is a fault in accepting [an offering] without having first offered it;
for whatever *caru* has been given to one’s own chosen deity, that is undoubtedly [efficacious].
[Likewise, so are] leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, drink, and medicine.
Even in times of distress, one should not eat that which has not been offered to me.

Through eating what has been offered [to me], one attains union [with me]. The yogi who is constantly intent on my worship, who eats only what has been offered to me, and who is devoted to meditation upon me, is fit for union with me. (23)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rites of Invocation and so forth," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Makutāgama.
The Kriyāpāda is completed.
This is the first chapter in the Caryāpāda:
the Blessed One, Mahādeva Maheśvara, who dwells on Mount Kailāsa.
[He approached] the supreme Great Compassionate One, whose abode is Mahākailāsa. || 1 ||
The god who has five faces on each of his five heads, adorned with fifty arms,
consisting of the five Brahmans, peaceful, and devoted to the fivefold cosmic functions.
Having beheld the Supreme Śiva and bowed down with humility,
he, filled with compassion and desiring to bestow grace upon the worlds, questioned him in this manner.
Rudra said:
O support of the entire universe, O supportless one, O supreme beyond the supreme, O primordial source of all principles, O Śrī Devadeva, salutations be unto you!
In the glorious and divine Āgamas as well as in the Vedas,
the Śāmbhava vow has been clearly prescribed by you as that which grants swift liberation.
"O twice-born one, tell me of the ritual for the final departure of those who are devoted to its practice, who bear the *liṅga*, and who are practitioners of true devotion. (6)
Paraśiva said:
Well asked by you, my child, who desire to uplift the world of devotees!
Listen, for I shall describe the supreme procedure regarding the final departure of devotees.
The concluding rite for those devoted to the Śāmbhava vow is that by which one,
once consecrated, may quickly attain liberation;
by which one, once consecrated, quickly enjoys the fulfillment of initiation.
By that very [means], even one who is devoid of devotion may attain the supreme goal, provided he is refined.
For those devoted to the Śāmbhava vow, whose bodies are in contact with their chosen liṅga,
the procedure for the Śiva-sacrifice has been declared in the Śruti for the attainment of my state.
(35) The etymological explanation of the term *śivamedha*:
"For those who have entered into me, Śiva, the *medha* (sacrifice) consisting of worship is known as the *śivamedha*; it should be performed by those seeking liberation."
This distinguished Pitṛmedha is remembered as the Śivamedha.
Even one devoid of devotion and knowledge attains the state of Śiva;
for every [element], there is the ground of "Pratiśiva," as well as water.
Thus the Śrutis indeed ordain meditative absorption for those whose yoga is devotion. 11.
Even one devoid of devotion and knowledge, or even one joined with great sin,
shall reach my state if he is consecrated by the sacrifice of Śiva.
He who doubts the attainment of liberation through devotion to me, the worship of my image, knowledge of me, and the Śāmbhava vow, will certainly go to hell. (13)
One who is intent on distrust, even regarding the Śāmbhavī vow and its concluding funeral rites,
is a fool who shall not emerge from hell.
Regarding the burning of the body of the Liṅga and its possessor:
that fool who burns the body of one observing the Śāmbhava vow shall be burned forever in hell by the servants of Yama. || 15 ||
(36) For the purification of my devotees who are embodied beings seeking liberation, the supreme method of meditative absorption (samādhi) has been fully described in the Pitṛmedha. || 16 ||
For men who are solely attached to their actions and subject to rebirth,
I have indeed prescribed the concluding rite as one refined by cremation.
O child, for those virtuous ones who are attached to the limbs of the Liṅga and are joined with non-return,
the supreme rite of final dissolution (avasāna-vidhi), refined by meditative absorption (samādhi), has been proclaimed.
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic,
if one who has fulfilled his vows dies, his body must not be cremated.
For those steadfast in the Śāmbhava vow, the state of being a preta does not exist; for those steadfast in the Śāmbhava vow, the state of being a preta is indeed not found.
For one liberated from the state of a preta, the loss of ritual action (karmalopa) is not to be feared.
The prohibition against the *apasavya* (left-hand) mode:
for those who possess the nature of the *liṅga*, the *apasavya* rite is not appropriate.
Therefore, one should not apply any of the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) to those belonging to the Śāmbhava [tradition]. || 21 ||
(37) For the Vīraśaivas, the refinement of samādhi is itself samādhi; this dharma of liberation sublates all other dharmas.
Therefore, when one is refined by samādhi, the loss of dharma is not to be feared. || 22 ||
The cultivation of meditative concentration directly bestows my presence;
burning [the body] is renowned in the world as the sole means for attaining the realm of the ancestors. (23)
I have ordained meditative absorption for the bodies of my devotees;
however, those in this world who are certainly faithless toward the methods taught by me shall never emerge from the ocean of hell.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Praise of the Śāmbhava Final Rite," in the Caryāpāda of the illustrious Makutāgama. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
Rudra said: O Supreme Lord, Soul of All, Eternal Cause of Everything!
Listen to me regarding that which must be performed immediately by one who desires to rise up. || 1 ||
Paraśiva said:
One who desires to rise up [from worldly existence] should immediately desire the bath of ashes and so forth, having fixed his consciousness upon me.
In order to perform acts such as giving gifts, one should perform the ablution beginning with that pertaining to Agni.
Having bathed in ghee and wearing clean garments, seated upon the ground on a seat of kusha grass,

and having applied the smearing of sacred ash (uddhūlana) and the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) with the ashes as prescribed, one should indeed wear rudrākṣa beads on the head, neck, hands, and other parts of the body.
If even one who wears ashes and rudrākṣas dies [while wearing them], he too attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, for humans and others?
p. 39) Then, having recognized through signs that death is imminent, one should internalize the fires within oneself with the mantra "O Agni, go" (*yāte agne*).
Taking the ashes and rubbing them with the mantra beginning with "Agni is... (*agnir iti*), one should touch the limbs. || 5 ||
The son of one whose time of death was unknown must perform the rites of giving and so forth;
furthermore, if that person who was unaware of his time should attain a departure from life,
his son must quickly perform the ritual of self-identification according to the rules.
Indeed, for the pacification of this fire superimposed upon the self,
a fire-oblation (homa) must immediately be performed in water by means of the purification of the six paths.
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself and performed the oblation in water,
he should give gold according to his ability, as well as a cow and a linga.
For you, who have set out for the supreme transcendence in order to achieve the successful departure through bliss, I bestow this cow known as "Transcendence."
For the sake of attaining union with Śiva, which is free from rebirth, I bestow upon you this most purifying Śivaliṅga. (10)
One who desires the excellence of a gift must certainly give a good sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
O Śaṅkara, everything deficient in a sacrificial fee becomes useless.
O Lord, whatever fruit is obtained by the gift of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas),
that same fruit one attains through the gift of a Śiva-liṅga. || 12 ||
One should constantly contemplate the dissolution of the gross body, together with all its limbs as the *liṅga*, until death itself,
with focused attention for the sake of attaining union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva. (13)
One should likewise join the principles (tattvas), such as "of life-force, the vital breath," and so forth;
one should dissolve the gross body into the causal elements in their proper sequence.
One perceives the cavities of the body in space, the continuity of breath in the wind,
heat in fire, and blood, pus, phlegm, and so forth in water.
Having thus dissolved the hard parts, such as bone and flesh, upon the ground as they arise, one should likewise dissolve the gross body and the subtle body as well. (16)
O Wielder of the Trident, listen also to the dissolution of the subtle body;
therein, the deities hold primacy by virtue of being the impellers of the organs.
Having observed them there, one should join the sense organs with their respective objects. || 17 ||

One should dissolve speech along with its objects of expression into Agni; the two hands together with their crafts into Indra; the feet along with movement into Viṣṇu; the generative organ along with sexual pleasure into Prajāpati;
and the anus along with the act of excretion into Mṛtyu; one should dissolve [all these] into Śarva.
One should dissolve the ear along with sound into the quarters; the skin along with tactile sensations into the wind; and the eye along with form into the sun.

One should dissolve the tongue into Varuṇa along with taste, the sense of smell into the two Aśvins along with fragrances, the mind into the Moon along with the objects of thought, the intellect into the Four-faced One (Brahmā) along with the objects of cognition, and the ego into Rudra along with the objects of ego-formation. || 20 ||
One should join the field-knower (kṣetrajña) with modifications such as being the enjoyer and so forth;
and one should join the mind with the objects of thought, which are the deities described as the effects of the qualities (guṇas).
One should then join that [mind], though it possesses modifications, into me, Brahman. (21)

The dissolution occurs in sequence, each into its own cause, of those known as earth and the other elements, ego, the Great One (mahat), and the Unmanifest (avyakta), which serve as the causes of transformation.

One should constantly contemplate the union of all limbs and the liṅga until the moment of death; one should cultivate this with focused attention for the sake of attaining union (sāyujya) with me. 23.
In all limbs, everywhere, at all times, and facing in all directions—
that Liṅga which is known through the instruction of the Guru shines forth.
This one supreme Liṅga alone is well-established within this body;
it shines forth in every direction through the nature of name, form, and action.
(43) The contemplation of the *iṣṭaliṅga* and the others:
the *iṣṭaliṅga* is in the external limb (*bāhyāṅga*), the *prāṇaliṅga* likewise within;
and the *bhāvaliṅga* is firmly established in this very way in the limb of the Self (*ātmāṅga*). || 26 ||
The Great Liṅga is in the limb of the heart; the Prasādaka Liṅga is in the limb of the ears;
the Caraliṅga is in the limb of the skin; and the Śivaliṅga is in the limb of the eyes.
The Guru-liṅga is indeed on the member of the tongue, and likewise on the member of the nose;
the Ācāra-liṅga is constantly well-established.

Just as the subtle body (liṅga) is established in the limbs of the organs of cognition in their respective order, so too is the subtle body established in the limbs of the organs of action in their respective order. || 29 ||
Inconceivable, indefinable, beyond the reach of consciousness and speech, though possessing all powers, omniscient, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 30 ||
Contemplating the performance of the expiation with a mind purified by that very intention, he approaches;
having then obtained permission from the community, he should perform the expiation. (31)

(44) Even the greatest sins accumulated throughout all previous births perish at that very moment here by means of the Liṅga, the Jaṅgama, the Guru’s feet, and the drinking of the holy water (tīrtha); no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (32)
For my devotees who are established in the great Śaiva vow, especially,
there is no other primary means of atonement except for the drinking of my sacred water.
But at the time of death, whoever has the water from my feet placed in his mouth—
even if he is devoid of proper conduct— he too attains a good destination;
likewise, one should recite my names with focused attention.
He who, at this final moment of his life, abandons his body while uttering "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva" three times;
The former sound becomes the cutter of the fears of existence, while those other two do not; they merely provide benefit to the imagined self.
At the time of death, the recitation of mantras should take place; then, the sons and others should cause the ear-mantras to be heard.
They should whisper the six-syllable mantra into the right ear, and likewise the eternal Niṣads.
Then, at the time of departure, one should also kindle camphor while reciting the mantra "aṇuḥ panthāḥ" for the purpose of traveling by way of the path beginning with light (arcis).
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Intention to Rise," in the Caryāpāda of the Śrīmakutāgama.
The third chapter.
Rudra said:
O you who transcend the universe, O source of the world, O support of all, O supreme beyond the supreme!
Having seen the departure [of the soul], tell me then what must be done by the performer [of the rite]. || 1 ||
Paraśiva said:
Having examined one whose vital breath has departed, the performer, with a purified consciousness, shall bathe, apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and be adorned with rudrākṣa beads. || 2 ||
For the sake of attaining authority over ritual acts, having performed the salutation to the Gaṇas for the sake of attaining authority over ritual acts,
one should receive their permission by making offerings according to one's capacity. || 3 ||
The gift given on the anniversary of the death-day excels all gifts given on festive occasions;
therefore, one who desires the welfare of the ancestors should give wealth according to their capacity.
(47) When a fault has occurred, one should perform the expiation for the occurrence of such things as being defiled by the remains of food;
one should provide a substitute for the Prājāpatya penance, consisting of wealth as prescribed.
If death occurs upon a bedstead, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
or else, one should give a cow or gold for the removal of that fault.
If death occurs at night, during the dark fortnight, or during the southern solstice,
one should perform the funeral rites after offering six oblations with the "Tāḥ sūryāḥ" verses.
Having consecrated the dissolved body of the vital breath with the Śrī Rudra mantra,
one should adorn the chosen liṅga with sacred ash, rudrākṣas, perfumes, and other ornaments.
Having placed it in his hand, worshipped it, and set it within a casket,
he established that form in the celestial chariot amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments.
(48) The names of the bearers of the celestial chariot are Mahokṣa, Vṛṣabha, Nandīśa, and Nandikeśvara.
One should choose four such bearers endowed with these names. 10.
The son should be led toward Śivārāma by those attendants and carriers;
in front [should go] auspicious musical instruments, and immediately after them, the ritual requisites.
The ritual substances, the consecrator, the celestial chariot, and the kinsmen follow in sequence. || 11 ||
Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (nivītin), these bearers shall carry that palanquin;
and even the kinsmen may go along, calling out "Niṣada! (O you who sit down).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Instruction on Samādhi," in the Caryāpāda of the glorious Makuṭāgama.
The Fourth Chapter.
Rudra said:
O You who are adorned by the splendor of the majestic play of infinite powers!
O Lord, tell me in its entirety that ritual procedure for the burial of wealth underground.
Paraśiva said:
Regarding the designation of the place for samādhi: it should be either near a temple of Śiva or in the vicinity of a grove dedicated to Śiva.
Near a sacred ford of Śiva, at the root of a bilva tree, or on a riverbank, a wise man should perform samādhi; listen as I describe its characteristics. || 2 ||
The method of arranging the *samādhi*:
it is four-cornered, with five steps, both long and wide;
the first excavation consists of nine squares, and the staircase has a single step.
The second is declared to have two feet, and likewise the third has three feet.
And to the south of that, a vedikā with three pādas should be made;
it should be triangular, consisting of three pādas, long and extended.

Having dug [the ground] with the thought, "May it not harm you," and having smeared it with cow-dung, and having adorned it with colored lines, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra. (5)
Having properly prepared the bed of ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should scatter leaves and flowers in the four directions, above and below.
Having placed the six syllables upon the body during meditative absorption and having consecrated it with the root mantra,
he moves even while the fourfold musical instruments play and a rain of flowers falls upon those [remains].
Reciting the sections beginning with "cittiḥ pṛthivyagniḥ," he should then place that body, facing north in the form of a svastika posture,
into the cavity [of the linga] with the words, "O Śambhu, accept the oblation."
Reciting "Ṛtaṃ tapa" (Truth and austerity), one should thereafter fill [the cavity] up to the neck with ashes, salt,
and earth.
With the mantra "sarvasya pratiśiva" and also with "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," one should place water, ashes, and a lump of clay upon the head of the deceased father;
thereafter, one should fill the pit with both ashes and earth. (10)
One should first cause the clothing to be put on, followed by a bath with one's garments; then one should perform the ritual bath.
Having bathed again with one's garments, one should then have the hair and beard shaved. (11)
Various sins, such as killing a Brahmin or stealing gold, reside depending upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair.
"Various sins as great as Mount Meru and Mandara reside depending upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair.
Reciting this mantra, one should have the hair and beard shaved. 13.

(52) He whose crest is like the crest of fire—that is, he who possesses a crest consisting of knowledge—is called a "crested one" (śikhin), namely the wise man; others are merely wearers of hair. (14)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Method of Samādhi," in the Caryāpāda of the venerable *Makuṭāgama*.
The fifth chapter.
Rudra said:
O ocean of beginningless, endless, and infinite auspicious qualities!
Now learn from me also the rites that follow immediately after the burial of the body.
Paraśiva said:
At the site of Samādhi, one should perform the installation and worship of the Liṅga together with the Bull;
having bathed after shaving the head, and adorned with sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads.
Then, having obtained his father's permission for the sake of attaining a divine form, he [departed]. || 2 ||
The son should install the Liṅga, adorned with five or nine bulls and inscribed with the names of the ancestors, in a state of meditative concentration.
Then, one should respectfully give the ten gifts, beginning with cows,
and should also worship the Liṅga installed in meditative absorption along with the bull.
O Maheśvara, for the sake of pacifying the heat produced by activities such as kneading clay pots, one should satisfy the desired liṅgas and other objects with milk.

One should offer three handfuls of water to one's father every day; however, one who desires the welfare of the ancestors must never give clothing, water for washing the feet, or similar offerings. (6)
Having entered the house together with his kinsmen and accompanied by a lamp,
the son should perform the rite of worship known as *nagnapracchādana* (the covering of the naked). || 7 ||
The protection of the *liṅga* installed by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for up to ten days:
"One should not move the *liṅga* installed by means of meditative absorption for ten days.
If it has been moved by insects or other such causes, one should place it back in its original position. (8)
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and touched that [liṅga], one should mutter the Vyāhṛtis;
if it has perished in its own form, one should install it again according to the rules.
The sequence for attaining the divine body occurs through the practice of the first chapter, whereby his crown is born;
through the practice of the second chapter, the nostrils, ears, and eyes [are perfected]. (10)
On the third day, the neck, chest, and arms also appear;
on the fourth day, these—the region of the navel, the penis, and the anus—come forth.
The two thighs would be formed on the fifth day, and skin would also appear on the sixth;
on the seventh day, all the veins are produced according to that same rule.
And on the eighth day, all the body hairs shall arise immediately thereafter;
by means of the ritual of the ninth day, his virility is produced.
Through the performance of the rites of the tenth day, his supreme satisfaction shall be attained;
thereafter, the propitiation of the Father, who possesses a divine form, must be performed.
By means of the ritual procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*, his state as Rudra arises;
furthermore, through the power of the conjunction with the principles (*tattvasaṃyojana*), his state as Maheśvara comes to be. || 15 ||
The procedure for the ninefold propitiation (*navārādhana*) should be performed on the first day, the third day, the fifth, the seventh,
as well as on the ninth and eleventh days. (16)

If either the new moon (darśa) or a solar transit (saṃkrānti) should occur within nine days [of the death], then another son may complete the rite, but the biological son shall not complete it. || 17 ||
The Procedure for Initiating an Uninitiated Father and Son:
However, at the time of the death of the parents, if the son is devoid of initiation, his funeral rites (antyakriyā) must be performed after entrusting the agency of the performer to the son. (18)
If the father is uninitiated, there is no consecration for that [uninitiated] soul.

Having invoked him into the *kūrca* grass and bestowed initiation upon him as prescribed, one should then properly perform the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and carry out the daily rites and so forth. (19)
If the father’s father or his grandfather has died without having received initiation, one should perform initiation for him in absentia (parokṣa) in order to achieve oneness with the father. (20)
Having brought a tuft of grass onto the sacrificial ground and having invoked the deceased by name,
he certainly becomes a possessor of the marks (liṅgin) through the performance of initiation in absentia.

On the tenth day, the relatives— those younger than the seventh generation— should perform the shaving, the milk-offering, the satiation-rite (tarpaṇa), and so forth; on that tenth day, they all, together with the performers of the rite, shall always carry out these acts.
Having bathed and applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they should perform the libation with milk;
thereafter, one should diligently offer the ten gifts according to one's capacity.
Having dismissed the *liṅga* together with the bull, and likewise having placed the *samādhi-liṅga* along with the bull upon a cloth,
one should bring it to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and, remaining self-controlled, discharge it there.

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation for a holy day (puṇyāhavācana), and so forth, and having removed the [linga] and bathed with water containing sesame seeds and myrobalan fruits, one should perform the fire-oblation known as Gāṇapatya and that named Ānanda. (25)
One should perform [the rite] together with the groups of ancestors for the attainment of supreme bliss;
having performed the recitation for the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), one should then proceed toward home.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Installation of the Liṅga and Other Matters," in the Caryāpāda of the Śrīmakutāgama.
The Sixth Chapter.
Rudra said:
O support of immeasurable qualities, the singular ocean of consciousness and bliss!
O Treasure of Compassion, please tell me what should be performed on the eleventh day.
Paraśiva said:
Regarding the rites of the eleventh day: having bathed on the eleventh day and having invited the devotees of Maheśa, one should perform the following.
Having first performed the Rudra-homa, one should carry out the rite of releasing the bull.
One should release a white bull, or one that is red or even blue,

for the sake of attaining my presence through the satisfaction of Nandikeśa; however, once the Siddha-hermitage, which is endowed with all enjoyments, has been attained, one should not release a bull.
There are sixteen modes of worship, beginning with the primary monthly ones; likewise,
there is the worship of the host of Rudras and that known as the release of the bull (vṛṣotsarga).
(60) One should perform the worship of the fifty Rudras, which relies upon the six locations of the six marks beginning with conduct;
one should practice this unsurpassed worship of the fifty Rudras. || 5 ||
In the eleventh month, the first *ūnamāsika* (intercalary monthly rite) occurs;

the *traipakṣika* (three-fortnightly rite) occurs at the third fortnight; likewise, the *ūnaṣāṇmāsika* (six-month intercalary rite) occurs at six months; and there is the monthly rite on the anniversary of death every month, as well as the *ūnābdika* (annual intercalary rite)—thus making sixteen rites in total.
On the eleventh day, one should indeed perform the sixteenfold adorations;
then, on the twelfth day, the son should perform the union with the ultimate reality (tattvasaṃyojana).
The definition of the *ekoddiṣṭa* [rite] is as follows:
that which is performed with reference to a single individual by means of the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure for the sake of attaining union with reality (*tattva*) is proclaimed as the *ekoddiṣṭa*. (8)
p. 61) Regarding the worship of Śiva, things to be avoided are as follows:
the Viśvedevas are not worshipped; the ritual of *abhiśravaṇa* is not mentioned; there is no circumambulation, no ritual dismissal (*visarga*), and no going to the boundary (*sīmānta*). || 9 ||
On the eleventh day, there is the Māheśvara feast; one should well-feed eleven devotees of Maheśvara.
For this is declared to be the worship of Rudra according to one's means.
In that very same way, one should feed even a single person for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the rite of releasing a bull;
indeed, the propitiation through the release of a bull must be performed, for it is dear to me.
The procedure for the propitiation of Rudra,
which rests upon the six locations characterized by the six marks such as right conduct (ācāra) and so forth,
should be performed as the propitiation of the fifty Rudras beginning with Khaḍgeśa. 12.
Four, six, ten, as well as eleven, twelve, sixteen, and two—these are the [deities] residing in the six locations beginning with Ācāraliṅga. || 13 ||
(62) The fifty names of the Rudras are:
Khaḍgeśa, Bakeśa, Śveta, Bhṛṅgīśvara, Chagalaṇḍeśa, Dviraṇḍeśa, and Mahākālīśvara. || 14 ||
After that are Bhujaṅgeśa, Pīnākīśa, and Dārukeśa; thereafter Āṣāḍīśa is remembered, who is the Lord of Umā in his half-female form.
Daṇḍīśa, Śātrīśa, Mitreśa, Meṣeśa, Lohiteśvara, Śikhīśvara, Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, and Pañcāntakeśvara. || 16 ||
Śivottama, Ekarudra, Īśa, Kūrmeśa, Ekanetraka, Caturānaneśvara, Ājeśa, Śarva, and Someśvara; || 17 ||
Lāṅgalīśa, Saṃvartakeśa, he who is known as Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananteśa, Sūkṣmeśa, and thereafter Trimūrtīśa is remembered. || 18 ||
Likewise Amareśa, Arghyeśa, Bhārabhūteśvara, Atithīśa, Sthāṇvīśa, Hara, and Jhiṇṭīśvara; || 19 ||
Bhautikeśa, Sadyojāteśa, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūreśa, Mahāsena, Lakulīśa, and Śiveśvara—
these fifty Rudras are to be worshipped in their proper sequence. (20)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for the Duties of the Eleventh Day," in the Caryāpāda of the venerable Makuṭāgama.
The seventh chapter.
Rudra said:
O you who are endowed with all powers, O you who are exalted by all sovereign splendors!
O Lord, tell me in its entirety the complete procedure for the rites of the twelve-day sacrifice.
Paraśiva said:
The rites of the twelfth day are for the purpose of the cessation of the fourth state, through the cessation of the notion of being a living soul.
After the application of the principles (tattvas) and so forth, even the fourth [state] ceases.
Through the union with the Śiva-liṅga obtained via initiation from his guru,
the twice-born attained oneness with Śiva according to the maxim of the *dvirepha* insect.

p. 65) When one who was connected as a limb of the lineage has died and the twelfth day has arrived, one must not perform the *sāpiṇḍya* rite at all, because from that point on there is no longer the state of being a *preta*. || 4 ||
Those who know my scripture recognize that the identity with Śiva, attained at the time of initiation, has become manifest through the state of being a living soul (jīva). || 5 ||

Having gathered the *kalās* corresponding to the number of the principles (*tattva*) from the ancestors who are non-different from Sadāśiva and the others, and having worshipped them elsewhere according to the prescribed rule, [he should proceed].

The sequence for the application of the principles (tattva) and so forth is as follows: For the sake of removing the notion of being a living soul from one who is attached to the body of a deceased *liṅga*, and for the sake of achieving the unification of the three groups, the son [the disciple] should apply the principles and so forth. (7)
On the twelfth day, the performer, having invited the lords of Maheśa and obtained the permission of the Gaṇas, should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as follows.

In order to achieve the state of union with Śiva for his father, he will perform the application of the principles (tattvayojana) by means of his father’s own ancestors, who are of the nature of Maheśa and the other deities.
[He offered it] to the two Viśvedevas known as Nandikeśa and Mahākāla, and to his father, grandfather, and ancestors, who are the very embodiments of Maheśa and the other [forms of Śiva]. (10)
"Having first made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): 'I shall perform the propitiation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) and the thirty-eight digits (kalās),' [he proceeds]. (11)

Having invoked and fully worshipped the Viśvedevas, the ancestors and others, as well as the principles (tattvas) and the constituent parts (kalās), and desiring to perform the conjunction of the principles,
one should indeed offer the ten gifts, beginning with cows, in their proper order.
Then the performer, having taken a copper vessel containing unbroken grains (akṣata),
stands near Maheśa, positioned at the place designated for the ancestors and others.
Having caused the grandfather and the others to touch the vessel with their hands,
he invoked the grandfather and the rest, taking his place as a representative of the ancestors.
Reciting the mantras beginning with "I take refuge in Sadyojāta," one should indeed unite the lords of the principles (tattveśas), headed by Candraśekhara, with that [deity].
(67) While reciting the mantras beginning with "Ishana is the lord of all vidyas," one should sequentially join the digits (kalas), such as Shashini and the rest, therein. 16.
In order to exclude the fourth [ancestor], the procedure for offering the vessel is as follows:
having first offered that vessel to him who occupies the position of the father,
I now join the father into the place of the grandfather.
Speaking thus, he should indeed offer that vessel to the one belonging to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Saying, "I unite the grandfather, who is indeed the very form of Maheśa, with the great-grandfather," he should then offer that vessel, as before,
to the one who occupies the station of the great-grandfather and is devoted to Maheśvara.

Thereafter, saying, "I unite the great-grandfather, whose nature is that of Sadāśiva," he should immediately offer the vessel to him who is situated in that place, addressing him as the "great-great-grandfather. (19)
I unite that stainless one, whose nature is Śiva, my great-great-grandfather, with the formless, supreme Śiva-tattva. (20)
Speaking thus, one should contemplate this [breath] as dissolved within oneself;
by the method described in this way, the fourth [state] ceases.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Ritual for Twelve Days," in the Caryāpāda of the glorious Makuṭāgama.
The eighth chapter.
Rudra said:
O support of the entire world, O one worshipped by all the immortals!
O Omniscient Supreme Lord, please explain the procedure for miscellaneous rites.

Paraśiva said: While the paternal uterine brothers are performing the rites, if another should arrive from another place within the ten-day period, he should perform the rites for the elapsed days and then proceed.
Excluding the meditative absorption (samādhi), one should perform the remaining ritual action in conjunction [with others]. || 2 ||
Regarding the sequence for the procedure of the union with reality (*tattvasaṃyojana*):
even if the funeral rites (*pitṛkarman*) have been performed by the youngest son or another,
the son should nevertheless perform the offering of water and the union with reality.
The deed performed by the elder brother was not a separate action on the part of the younger brother.

p. 70) Regarding the specific rule for the application of the elements (*tattvayojana*) by the performer of the *śrāddha*: if the wife of the performer has become menstruating at the end of the period of impurity, he should perform the remainder of the *śrāddha* and then release the application of the elements. || 4 ||
If the *tattvasaṃyojana* rite has been performed when the wife is menstruating or deceased, that *tattvasaṃyojana* shall not take place; one should perform it on the fifth day.
There is no joining with the *tattva* for eunuchs and the like;
there is likewise no joining with the *tattva* for wicked women, nor for those who are under twelve years of age, nor for the deceased, nor for celibate students (*brahmacārin*). (6)
For lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and ascetics (yatī), there is likewise the Īśāna-bali;
however, for those devoid of the union with the Tattvas, the annual rite (pratyābdika) is not prescribed.
The Pārvaṇa worship and other rites, excluding those for the gods, which are equal to the Pārvaṇa rite and accompanied by the water-pot (udakumbha),
should be performed daily according to the procedure of formal resolve (saṃkalpa) until the end of the year.
After the performance of the *tattvasaṃyojana*, for one year or half of that time,
the son should perform no other *pārvaṇa* worship for the *aṣṭakā*.

p. 71) By virtue of the conjunction with the [supreme] reality, the son should perform for his father—who is endowed with the status of Maheśvara—every year and every month according to the pārvaṇa rite. || 10 ||
If one does not eat the remnants of the cooked food in rites for the gods or the ancestors, even if those rites have been properly performed, they shall be rendered fruitless for him. (11)
When a nocturnal vow has been undertaken, or during a time of distress, or upon the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse),
the Śrāddha should be performed even at night by those endowed with faith.
During an eclipse, on the anniversary of a paternal relative's death, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), on the new moon day, and during the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign,
the wise man should satiate the ancestors with pure water mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata).
The characteristic of propitiation is as follows:
when one's ancestors and others are propitiated with devotion there in the ancestral rite (paitṛka), that is declared to be propitiation (ārādhana). || 14 ||
In that regard, Nandin and Mahākāla are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas;
for the sake of the ancestors, these three—Maheśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva—are celebrated, while Śambhu is remembered as the protector. (15)

Śrāddha is of two kinds, and its constituent parts are likewise; indeed, Śrāddha is declared to be twofold: that which generates satisfaction for the Pitṛs residing in the world of the ancestors, and [that for] those dwelling in the world of the Pitṛs. || 16 ||
O Rudra, listen as I describe the constituent parts of the *śrāddha* in their proper order:

the fire-oblation (*homa*), the renunciation (*tyāga*), the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the Viśvedevas, sesame seeds (*tila*), *kuśa* grass, the invocation of the ancestors and gods, the water-offering vessel (*arghyapātra*), and the protector. (17)
And the scattering of food (vikira) with the sacred thread over the right shoulder is proclaimed as a constituent part of the Śrāddha;
O son, I shall now describe it for the sake of the Pitṛs who dwell in my world.
In the rite of Śrāddha, seven things are prohibited:

the fire-oblation (homa), the rice-balls (piṇḍa), sesame seeds, Darbha grass, the scattering of food (vikira), the water-offering vessel (arghyapātra), and the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya). These seven are forbidden in the Śrāddha ceremony.
The Viśvedevas, the renunciation intended for the ancestors, and the protector [of the rite] are indeed constituent parts of the Śrāddha; therefore, one should employ them. (20)
For those who observe the Śāmbhava vow, there is no *sapiṇḍya* (ancestral kinship).
He who performs a *śrāddha* with *sapiṇḍa* rites for one who observes the Śāmbhava vow will certainly cause his lineage up to the seventh generation to fall into hell. (21)

The propitiation of the Threefold Maṇḍala is said to be threefold: that pertaining to householders and others, that pertaining to those who have renounced worldly ties, and likewise that which is performed through mere resolve. || 22 ||
The rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras and other such texts, which is associated with the Viśvedevas and others,

must be performed excluding the Viśvedevas, the dedication to the ancestors (pitṛs), the formal renunciation (tyāga), and likewise the protector; this is the procedure for one who has no wife and lacks the [usual] authority.

Having omitted the Viśvedevas, the protector, the renunciation (tyāga), the invocation (āvāhana), and so forth, the rite for those of compassionate nature is prescribed by means of mere mental resolve (saṃkalpa) alone. || 24 ||

In the matter of propitiation, [the officiant] should be a worshiper of Maheśvara, one who is thoroughly conversant with the Śaiva scriptures, skilled in the knowledge of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala),
devoted to the three daily rites of worship, and dedicated to the realization of the Liṅga. || 25 ||
One who is devoted to the worship of Maheśvara is considered the foremost in terms of propitiation;
one who is intent on worshipping him once a day is proclaimed as mediocre. (26)
He who eats what has not been offered, who does not worship the Liṅga even once,
and who hates my devotees— he should always be avoided.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Miscellaneous Rites," in the Caryāpāda of the Śrīmakutāgama.
The ninth chapter begins with Rudra saying:
O Lord of the Universe, you who are undisturbed by the vast web of worlds fashioned through your own divine play,
tell me the complete procedure for my annual rites.
Paraśiva said:
Having performed the rites of daily obligation and the procedure for the annual worship, he respectfully summoned the Brahmins.
Having lit a lamp, adorned [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, and having prostrated, || 2 ||
Having taken betel-leaf along with ashes, a *ghuṇṭikā*, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
one should pay obeisance to Nandikeśa and the other lords of the Gaṇas.
Then, with a steady mind, one should perform a circumambulation while reciting "Obeisance to the non-disease-inflicting ones" (nama āvyādhinībhyaḥ) three times, making the sound of a bell.

Then, having sipped water and proclaimed the place and time in their proper order, and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the worship known as the 'Unification Day' of my father, which is the means for his satisfaction," he should also worship the ritual pitcher (kalaśa).
p. 76) "These [substances] cause the destruction of evil for the sake of the worship of Maheśa.
Having thus consecrated the materials with water, one should offer the *kṣaṇas* in due order. (6)

One should avoid seven things in the Śaiva rite: the avoidance of the seven substances, the counter-clockwise circumambulation, sesame seeds, darbha grass, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the fire-ritual, the scattering of offerings (vikira), and the arghya vessel. Thus, one should renounce these seven.
The deities for the propitiation of the ancestors are as follows:
the father is said to be Maheśvara, his father is Sadāśiva, and the great-grandfather is Śiva; these are the deities for the propitiation of the ancestors.
In the act of propitiation, one must avoid partiality; those who are foremost through austerity or knowledge deserve the highest seat.
Partiality in giving gifts, providing food, or performing worship does not bring about auspicious results.
(77) By the offering of flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, there is the invitation of Maheśvara;
likewise at the station of the Viśvedevas known as Nandin and others, and also at the station of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) known as Maheśvara and others. (10)
Having offered flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and moments of time at the place of Śambhu, the Protector, he should also say: "May your favor be bestowed."
Those who have been invited should remain observant of silence, with their minds absorbed in meditation on me;
they should live contented, for if they do not, they shall fall into hell.
One should fashion two mandalas for the worship of the feet, either external or internal;
likewise, one enters the two mandalas with the mantra *araṅgama*.
Between those two, in the middle, a space of six finger-breadths must indeed be made,
so that there may be no contact with the water for the feet between the ancestors and the gods.
Having prepared two mandalas for the purpose of offering water for the feet to the ancestors and the deities,
one should worship them in those places with ashes, scents, and all other offerings.
Having welcomed the invited devotees of Maheśvara by inquiring after their well-being and offering them seats,
one should then wash their feet while reciting the verse "śanno devīḥ. (16)
Having sprinkled the water from his feet upon his own head and having rubbed his feet with a cloth,
[he should worship them] with ashes, unbroken grains (akṣata), perfumes, flowers, bilva leaves, and so forth.

One should worship the Viśvedevas, the ancestors, and then the protector in due order with incense, lamps, food offerings, and mantra-offerings of flowers. Then both the performer and the eaters should wash their feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then, having restrained his breath, the performer, taking the unbroken rice grains (akṣata) from the hand-vessel,
should offer the seats (viṣṭara) while reciting "svāhā" and "svadhā."
The invocation of the Viśvedevas and others:
Having invoked the Viśvedevas and the ancestors by name and lineage,
and having worshipped them in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
And one should satisfy him well with garments and gold according to one's ability. || 20 ||
Having scattered ashes over the foods while reciting "O Maheśa," and having meditated upon the god Maheśvara during the act of worship at Gayā,
one should then perform the worship after visualizing the ancestors beginning with Maheśa. || 21 ||
Having recited the mantra "māheśvarebhyo bhojanaparyaveṣaṇam" for the sake of removing defects in the cooking,
one should sprinkle clarified butter over the food with the mantras known as the five Brahmans.
One may place an adequate amount of food, both solid and soft, into the vessels; furthermore, there is the practice of placing the thumb upon the *prasāda*,
which constitutes the rite of offering one's own favorite *liṅga* to the Great Lord.
Reciting "kartā deva savitā," he performs the sprinkling around;
having done so for the vessel, he says, "pṛthivī te pātraṃ yacchaṃyoḥ. (24)
Then one should recite the *tryambaka* mantra, which bestows the grace of Maheśvara;
having taken hold [of the water], one should place the thumb therein with a serene mind. (25)
With the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā*, he performs the libation for the gods and the ancestors, while contemplating the eater, the food, and himself as Brahman;
likewise, he contemplates the earth as Gayā and the wielder of the trident as the eater. (26)

Having pronounced the name and the lineage, as well as the relationship and the expression of devotion, he should offer [the oblation] to the gods and the ancestors in due order, uttering "svāhā," "svadhā" as appropriate, "namas," and "not mine. (27)
Regarding the description of the satisfaction of ancestors that is free from rebirth:

"May what is given at Gayā, at the feet of Śrī Rudra, and at sacred sites such as Śrīnaga and others, be [efficacious]"—uttering these words, one should indeed release water along with unbroken grains (akṣata). (28)
Then, by forming a resolve and performing the worship with a single meal,
the ancestors obtain inexhaustible satisfaction that is free from rebirth.
Saying, "May there be the eternal attainment of union with Śiva," he should cause [the patron] to recite, "May all this be given at the proper time. (30)
The sequence for offering the *āpośāna* water:
Having offered the *āpośāna* to the gods and the ancestors in due order, [one should know that] Mahādeva Maheśvara, as Īśāna, exists in the form of the ancestors. (31)
"May the Blessed Lord Īśa, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva, be pleased;
may the Lord in the form of the ancestors be pleased"—having spoken thus, one should pour out water.
Having made the prayer to Maheśvara,
they should offer oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with the mantras beginning with "In faith,
O Prāṇa," while reciting three times, "The wind is honey," and "Honey."
Having said, "Enjoy [it] as you please," he should cause them to respond.
Whatever action is performed in the midst of a mantra or in the midst of a ritual, preceded by the remembrance of Śambhu, that becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
One should accept what is desired, request what is needed, and discard what is not desired;
then, sitting at ease with a tranquil mind, one should eat. (35)
Having spoken thus to those hosts of Niṣādas at the time for the enjoyment of his favor,
he should also cause them to hear the mantras for the consecration of the sacrificial ladle, beginning with those of Jābāla.
For them, the *uttarāpośana* rite occurs at the end of the consumption of the prasāda, with the mantra "madhu vātā" and the word "madhu.
Having said to them, "Are you satisfied? he should cause them to say, "We are satisfied. (37)
Having given the *uttarāpośana* water and immediately after the purification of the hands, he should cause [the disciple] to recite the subsequent mantras, beginning with "In faith, O Prāṇa. (38)
The Person, indeed, is the size of a thumb and dwells within the thumb;
as the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, he brings satisfaction.
Having said, "This is the sequence of performance after the meal," and having caused them to recite the benedictions, the inexhaustible [offering],
and the propitiation, he recited, "For the Ṛgveda thee" and "The earth is peace."
Having circumambulated them three times clockwise and having caused them to pronounce "svāhā" and "svadhā," he should then speak of the ritual services as is appropriate. (41)
Today my birth has become fruitful through the prostration at your feet;
today, by your grace, all those born of my lineage have gone to heaven.
"You have been troubled in such a manner by the giving of leaves, branches, and so forth;
therefore, forgetting that collection of hardships in your hearts, you should grant me forgiveness.
Having thus prostrated before them, he should again receive their blessings. (43)

May the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas) of men, out of affection, grant long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness; likewise, may they bestow sovereignty upon those devoted to Maheśvara by accepting their words of benediction.
Having spoken thus, one should follow the departing Brahmins as far as the boundary.
In the worship of Mahālaya as well as in the worship at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) alone may differ; there shall be no difference in the actual performance (prayoga).
p. 84) Regarding the sequence for propitiating the ancestors and others in the *śrāddha* rite:
in the annual rites (*pratyābdika*), there may be a group consisting of either the mothers or the fathers;
