however, in the *mahālaya* propitiation and similar rites, all [ancestors] beginning with the father are prescribed. || 46 ||
First the father, and likewise the mother, as well as the stepmother; then the maternal grandfathers with their wives, and immediately after them, one's own wives. (47)
The son-in-law, brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles along with their wives;
the daughter, the sister, the son of a daughter, and the sister's son (48).
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the son-in-law, the brother-in-law, the daughter-in-law, the father-in-law, the brother-in-law, the master, the preceptor, and the heir. (49)
O Maheśvara, if Māheśvaras are not available, everything should be performed upon seats;
and if, despite every effort, Māheśvaras are entirely unavailable,
one should place either a bell or a small vessel of ashes upon the seats.
Then one should perform all forms of worship, beginning with the worship of the feet.
One should give food to the cow and also a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins;
by acting in this way, one obtains the great fruit of propitiation. (51)
Regarding the description of the fruit of propitiating one's parents:
"He who performs the propitiation of his parents according to this rite, having obtained long life, prosperity, and progeny, is glorified in the world of Śiva. (52)
There is a fault in non-performance;
he who does not perform [this] thus, whether out of atheism or laziness, having passed through a hundred births as a crow, is indeed born as a dog. (53)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Annual Ritual," in the Caryāpāda of the Śrīmakutāgama.
The Tenth Chapter.
Rudra said:
O support of the entire universe, O supportless one, O ocean of compassion!
O Lord, I have a certain doubt regarding the subject of impurity.
How can there be any connection with impurity for those who observe the vow, whose bodies have been abandoned through the contemplation of the Divine, and who are purified by the Śāmbhava vow?
"How could there be a connection with impurity of the body for those who are immortal?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O sole ocean of all knowledge. (3)
Paraśiva said:
"Well asked by you, my child, who desire to favor true devotees!
Though it is a secret, I shall speak; listen with an attentive mind."
Even for those devoted to the Śāmbhava vow, there is the occurrence of impurity;
for those purified by the Śāmbhava vow, whose souls are intent on service to Me,
and who are partakers of liberation, there is contact with impurity caused by the casting off of the body.
Even though it is indeed impossible [to attain it] because of not disclosing the faults of living beings, (5)
Nevertheless, for those who possess bodies connected to saṃsāra,
there exists here impurity arising from the birth and destruction of the body;
for that [impurity] is indeed not applicable to ascetics (*yatis*), because they lack connection to saṃsāra.
Therefore, contact with the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is the cause for the occurrence of impurity;
conclude that because of such contact, there is impurity even for those who observe vows.
Even while impurity (āśauca) exists, there is no obstacle to worship; indeed,
even when impurity is present, there is no hindrance to my worship,
for my image cuts through obstacles by virtue of the power of initiation (dīkṣā).
Furthermore, regarding occasional rites,
daily rites, and other such actions, the contraction of the basis for impurity is indeed equal for those who have not received initiation.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires within himself as a drinker of Soma,
there will certainly be impurity among his kinsmen only upon his departure from the body.
Impurity (āśauca) is traditionally remembered as being of two kinds—birth and death—and also of four kinds:
slight, excessive, incomplete, and complete. (11)
That which lasts for a short time would be "small," while that which lasts for a long time would be "great.
That which lasts for three nights and so forth would be "incomplete," whereas that which lasts for ten days and so forth would be "complete. (12)
Regarding the period of impurity for kinsmen, a husband and wife, uterine brothers, and the various social classes (varṇas):
in the case of a miscarriage, the mother's impurity lasts three nights, while for the kinsmen it does not exist [beyond that].
In the case of a full-term birth, the mother's impurity lasts for a number of days equal to the months of pregnancy, while for the father and others it is three days.
Ten days are prescribed for a Brahmin, twelve days for a Kṣatriya, fifteen days for a Vaiśya, and one month is accepted for a Śūdra. (14)
When ten days have passed, the impurity arising from birth no longer exists;
however, upon hearing of a son's birth, one becomes pure by immersing oneself in water.
Upon the birth or death [of a relative], immediate purification is prescribed for kinsmen;
however, for a husband and wife, as well as for uterine brothers, it is by ten days alone.
Regarding the period of impurity for those who have died without teeth having grown:
"In the case of a child who has not yet cut its teeth, purification is ordained to be immediate;
however, for a boy whose tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has not been performed, it shall last for a single day and night. (17)

Prior to the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the impurity for the mother and father upon the death of an infant lasts for three nights; however, for those who have undergone initiation, full impurity is prescribed.
For kinsmen, the period of impurity shall be ten days; for those who offer libations of water (sodaka), it is three nights;
for those of the same lineage (sagotra), it is merely bathing; for others than these, none exists.
(p. 90) The rule for impurity regarding the death of maternal uncles and others:
"In the case of the death of maternal uncles and so forth, it is ordained that there be three nights [of impurity];
however, upon the death of other kinsmen, an impurity lasting for a 'pakṣiṇī' (two days with the intervening night) is declared. (20)

Up to three months, there shall be a fast of three nights; up to six months, however, it is a "pakṣiṇī" (two days with the intervening night); up to one year, it is a day and a night; beyond that, one becomes pure by bathing. || 21 ||
Purification from many periods of impurity occurs through a single performance (tantra);
for even when many [impurities] coincide, one is indeed purified by that same single performance.
Whether they are equal or even shorter, one should conclude them with the first [period]. || 22 ||
Regarding the precedence of impurity due to death:
"Whether a birth occurs during a period of death-impurity, or a death occurs during a period of birth-impurity—
if such a case arises, it is proclaimed that the death-impurity alone takes precedence."
However, the impurity resulting from the death of parents subverts any other impurity. (23)
If the mother should die during the ten-day period of impurity for the father,
one should complete the full period for the father and observe the *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) for the mother.
The procedure for purification when following a corpse:
Having followed a corpse belonging to a kinsman or even another, a Brahmin becomes pure simply by bathing, smearing himself with ashes, and looking at the sun. (25)
For those who have reached the final goal and others, there is no impurity; for lifelong students, forest-dwellers, ascetics, and celibate students,
no impurity arising from birth or death exists here.
The rule for immediate purification is prescribed in cases of giving gifts, marriage, sacrifice, battle, national upheaval,
and even in times of dire distress. (27)
The twilight worship (sandhyā-pūjā) must never be abandoned, even during periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka). One should not forsake the twilight worship;
rather, one should perform the silent (upāṃśu) twilight worship by means of all three instruments [of body, speech, and mind]. (28)
Conclusion of the Text:
I have thus briefly declared the duties of those who observe the Śāmbhava vow.
Those who possess faith are liberated; others, being deluded, only suffer. (29)
My Dharma-śāstra, the Makuṭa, which has become like a crown [to me], should be studied with diligence by one who desires my grace. (30)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for Impurity," in the Caryāpāda of the latter section of the glorious Makuṭāgama. || 10 ||
And this Makuṭāgama is completed.
